name: Nuclear & SMR timelines
description_md: Nuclear is the power source hyperscalers actually want — firm, carbon-free, 24/7 — and the money is already committed (Microsoft/Crane, Google/Duane Arnold via NextEra, Meta/Clinton, Amazon/Talen, the $80B Westinghouse AP1000 government program). The bottleneck is time: nothing nuclear arrives when the demand is. The restart wave lands 2027-29 — Crane (ex-TMI Unit 1, ~835MW) targets 2027 with NRC environmental review clearing in June 2026; Duane Arnold (~615MW) targets Q1 2029; only Palisades (restarted Oct 2025) is already online. SMRs are a ~2030s technology: Holtec targets 2030 at Palisades, Oklo's first Aurora and the Amazon/X-energy and Google/Kairos units cluster late-decade, and no US SMR has yet produced a commercial watt. New AP1000s under the $80B Westinghouse program would deliver in the early-to-mid 2030s at best (Vogtle 3/4 took ~10 years). Against demand arriving 2026-28, nuclear is a claim on the future, not capacity — total restart pipeline is ~2.2GW versus data-center demand growing 5-7GW/year. Status basis: judged watch, not binding — nuclear isn't a rationed input the buildout queues for (gas and grid are); it is a timing mismatch worth tracking because slippage in 2027-29 restarts would push more demand onto the already-binding gas-turbine and grid constraints.

controlled_by.share_note: Largest US nuclear fleet (~55GW post-Calpine); owns the Crane 2027 restart and most uprate potential (disclosed)
Sole US large-reactor vendor (AP1000); anchor of the $80B government fleet program (press_reported)
Leading listed SMR developer; ~14GW pipeline incl. 12GW Switch agreement — all pre-operational (company_claimed)

dependents.dependency_md: 20-year PPA for Crane's ~835MW; power flows only if the 2027 restart holds — until then Microsoft's carbon-matching and capacity plans lean on grid power.
PPA with NextEra for Duane Arnold (~615MW, Q1-2029) plus Kairos SMR agreement (~500MW, 2030+); both are late-decade capacity against near-term load.
$18B/1,920MW Susquehanna PPA (existing plant — the exception that works now) plus X-energy SMR program (~2030s).
>2.6GW of nuclear PPAs (Clinton, Vistra PJM units) — mostly preserving existing plants rather than adding new capacity before 2030.

substitutes_md: For the 2026-29 gap: gas turbines (themselves 4-5 years booked), fuel cells, gensets, and grid purchases — i.e., the other bottlenecks in this registry. Existing-plant PPAs and co-location (Susquehanna/Talen, Clinton) are the only nuclear that works on AI timelines, and that supply is nearly fully claimed. Uprates at existing reactors (~2-5% each) add sub-GW quantities. Restart candidates beyond the current three are scarce — few shuttered plants remain restartable. Internationally, Korean APR1400s and Chinese builds prove speed is possible (~6-7 years) but do not serve US load.
downcycle_md: Nuclear deals are the most protected layer in an AI downturn — and the least exposed to glut: PPAs are 15-20-year utility-grade contracts with investment-grade counterparties, and the plants serve the grid regardless of AI demand (Susquehanna/Crane power resells into PJM at worst). The parties bearing AI-specific risk are the SMR developers: pre-revenue, funded by equity priced on multi-GW pipelines of largely non-binding master agreements (Oklo's 12GW Switch deal is an agreement to negotiate orders, not take-or-pay), so a demand fall would repric them violently — as the 2023 NuScale/UAMPS cancellation previewed. The Westinghouse program's government backstop (US takes 20% of distributions above $17.5B) socializes upside and cushions downside. Restarts under construction would complete regardless; uncommitted AP1000 orders would quietly not materialize.

observations.metric_label: Restart pipeline capacity (Palisades + Crane + Duane Arnold)
observations.method_md: Sum of Palisades ~800MW (restarted Oct 2025), Crane ~835MW (target 2027), Duane Arnold ~615MW (target Q1 2029) from company/NRC disclosures.
observations.notes: Versus US data-center load growth of ~5-7GW/year — the whole restart wave covers under half a year of demand growth.
Announced ≥$80B AP1000 fleet with Commerce Dept; US government takes 20% of distributions above $17.5B. Headline commitment — no reactor from this program can deliver power before the early 2030s.

observations.method_md: Approximate minimum time-to-power for new nuclear commitments made in 2026: SMR first units target ~2030 (Holtec Palisades 'Mission 2030', Oklo, X-energy), i.e. ~48-72 months; new AP1000s longer (Vogtle 3/4 took ~120 months from construction start). Restarts are faster (~24-36 months) but the candidate pool is exhausted.
observations.notes: The structural mismatch: AI demand 2026-28 vs nuclear supply 2029-2035.
